Definition: Whether the instant payment system enables or plans to enable instant payments across national borders to other countries or regional payment systems, supporting remittances, trade, and regional integration.
Comments: Lesotho participates in SIRESS (SADC Integrated Regional Electronic Settlement System) as a regional RTGS settlement system, enabling cross-border settlement in the SADC region (systemically important FMI in CBL oversight framework). However, LeSwitch is described as domestic-only for cross-border transactions (press release notes cross-border transactions handled through existing systems). This indicates cross-border functionality exists (via regional RTGS) but not as an instant retail cross-border feature of LeSwitch. ([CBL Payment System Oversight Framework 2018](https://centralbank.org.ls/wp-content/uploads/Payment_System_Oversight_Framework_2018.pdf);[Standard Lesotho Bank press release](https://www.standardlesothobank.co.ls/lesotho/personal/About-us/press-releases/press-release-lesotho-national-payment-switch-leswitch)).
revision_notes: Original score of 4 (Partially functional) cited the 2018 CBL Payment System Oversight Framework and a 2024 Standard Lesotho Bank press release. Both sources fetched and read. The press release explicitly states LeSwitch (the domestic instant payment switch, launched March 2024) does not process cross-border transactions, which continue via 'existing payment systems'. The oversight framework and an additional CBL 2013 economic review confirm Lesotho has participated in SADC-RTGS (formerly SIRESS) since July 2013, a real-time interbank settlement system covering the Common Monetary Area and wider SADC region. The score of 4 is retained because cross-border real-time settlement capability genuinely exists, but this rests on interpreting the CMA-wide SADC-RTGS/SIRESS system as within scope of 'the instant payment system' rather than solely the newer domestic LeSwitch switch, which explicitly excludes cross-border. This interpretive question is flagged for human review rather than resolved unilaterally.
revised_comments: Lesotho's national instant payment system (LeSwitch), launched in March 2024, is explicitly designed for domestic transactions only, with cross-border payments continuing to be processed through existing channels. Lesotho nonetheless participates in the SADC Integrated Regional Electronic Settlement System (SADC-RTGS, formerly SIRESS), a real-time gross settlement system operating since July 2013 that settles interbank transactions across the Common Monetary Area and the wider SADC region. Cross-border payment capability therefore exists at the wholesale interbank level but is not yet integrated into the domestic instant retail payment infrastructure.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: Lesotho has payment-relevant consumer protection provisions through (i) mobile money guidelines requiring consumer protection measures (participant charter commitments, complaint/dispute avenues, transparency of fees, refund policies, etc.) and (ii) clearing rules that include dispute resolution procedures for EFT items (e.g., disputed items, reversal timelines). ([CBL Mobile Money Guidelines PDF](https://dfsobservatory.com/sites/default/files/Central%20Bank%20of%20Lesotho%20-%20Guidelines%20on%20Mobile%20Money.pdf);[EFT Rules PDF](https://centralbank.org.ls/wp-content/uploads/EFT_Rules.pdf)).
revision_notes: Original score of 3 (Yes) cited CBL Mobile Money Guidelines (link timed out on refetch, could not be independently re-verified) and the EFT Rules. The EFT Rules were fetched directly and confirmed to include a dispute resolution section (4.1.2) with reversal and fraud handling procedures. Additionally located and read the Payment Systems (Issuers of Electronic Payment Instruments) Regulations 2017, which contain a dedicated 'Consumer protection and recourse' section (s.33) requiring a user charter, complaint-handling procedures, a toll-free complaints line and dispute records. The score of 3 is confirmed on stronger, more current primary evidence than originally cited.
revised_comments: Digital payment consumer protection in Lesotho is anchored in the Payment Systems (Issuers of Electronic Payment Instruments) Regulations, 2017, which require e-money issuers to maintain a user charter covering safe operations, privacy, service reliability and transparency, alongside mandatory complaint-handling procedures, a dedicated toll-free complaints line, and record-keeping of disputes. The Electronic Funds Transfer Credit and Debit Clearing Rules administered by the Payment Association of Lesotho further set out dispute resolution and reversal procedures for EFT transactions. Together these instruments constitute a dedicated payment consumer protection framework.

Definition: Whether national data protection or privacy legislation exists and explicitly covers payment transaction data, including provisions on data collection, storage, sharing, retention, and user rights over their payment data.
Comments: Lesotho has a general Data Protection Act (commonly cited as Data Protection Act, 2011/2012 or 2013 in different reproductions) establishing data protection principles and a Data Protection Commission. ([ICT Policy Africa copy of Data Protection Act](https://ictpolicyafrica.org/api/documents/download?_id=5d9432b89b93fa001b80406f);[Lesotho Government Gazette copy via NIC](https://www.nic.ls/lsnic/community/policies/Data_Protection_Act_2011_Lesotho.pdf)). No evidence found of payments-specific data provisions beyond general personal data coverage.
revision_notes: Original score of 2 (General Data Protection Legislation) cited the Data Protection Act (dated variably 2011/2012/2013 across sources). Confirmed via LesLII as the Data Protection Act, 2011, Act No. 5 of 2012, gazetted 22 February 2012, a general data protection law with no payment-specific provisions on its face. Further searching located the Financial Consumer Protection Act, 2022, which per law-firm commentary on s.43 (primary gazette text not independently retrieved) explicitly extends and reinforces data protection obligations for financial institutions including payment service providers, with sector-specific safeguards taking precedence over the general Act and Central Bank enforcement powers for breaches. Combined with payment-specific confidentiality, audit-trail and KYC/CDD data provisions already fetched in the 2017 PSP Issuers Regulations, this supports raising the score to 3 (Specific Payment Data Provisions). This is a promotion to the top of the scale and rests partly on secondary commentary rather than a directly-fetched primary gazette text of the 2022 Act, so it is flagged for human review to verify the primary source before the score stands.
revised_comments: Lesotho's data protection regime rests on the Data Protection Act, 2011 (Act No. 5 of 2012), which establishes general principles for the collection, processing, storage and cross-border transfer of personal information and creates a Data Protection Commission. The Financial Consumer Protection Act, 2022 extends and reinforces these obligations specifically for financial institutions, including payment service providers: section 43 requires financial institutions to take full responsibility for personal information they collect and to process it in accordance with the Data Protection Act, and provides that stronger sector-specific safeguards prevail over the general Act. The Central Bank of Lesotho, as regulator, is empowered to enforce these data obligations directly against financial and payment institutions, including administrative penalties for breaches. Payment-specific instruments such as the Payment Systems (Issuers of Electronic Payment Instruments) Regulations, 2017 additionally impose confidentiality, audit-trail and KYC/CDD data-handling requirements on payment service providers.

Definition: Whether the scheme rules governing payment system participation, pricing structure, technical requirements, security standards, and conduct are publicly accessible via website, public repository, or on request. Transparency indicator.
Comments: CBL’s Payment Systems page provides public preview/download links to scheme rule documents (e.g., EFT Rules; MIACH Rules), indicating rules are publicly available online rather than confidential/on-request. ([CBL Payment Systems page](https://centralbank.org.ls/payment-systems-2/);[EFT Rules PDF](https://centralbank.org.ls/wp-content/uploads/EFT_Rules.pdf)).
revision_notes: Original score of 3 (Yes - Fully Public) cited the CBL Payment Systems page and EFT Rules. Both fetched and confirmed: the CBL Payment Systems page (centralbank.org.ls/payment-systems-2/) provides direct download links to the EFT Rules, MIACH Rules, Lesotho Wire Rule Book, Payment Systems Act 2014, PSP Issuers Regulations 2017 and the 2018 Oversight Framework, all accessible without registration or request. Score of 3 is confirmed on direct primary evidence.
revised_comments: The Central Bank of Lesotho publishes the core scheme rules governing its payment systems on its public website, including the Electronic Funds Transfer Credit and Debit Clearing Rules, the MIACH Rules, the Lesotho Wire Rule Book, the Payment Systems Act 2014, the Payment Systems (Issuers of Electronic Payment Instruments) Regulations 2017, and the National Payment System Oversight Framework 2018. These documents are downloadable directly from the Bank's Payment Systems page without registration or request, indicating a fully public disclosure regime.
